1. A top professional in experimental design would separate the result from the limits of the experiment, quantify uncertainty around the acceptance rate, and recommend a decision proportional to the evidence. They would check whether the 48 runs are independent and comparable, and whether the easy task set could plausibly detect a gain.

2. They would start from the run-level records: task, treatment/control assignment, accepted/rejected outcome, paid-token count, and any exclusions or retries—not a summary or recollection.

3. They would use a preregistered comparison where available; otherwise, document the analysis choices. Compare acceptance rates with confidence intervals and paid-token distributions with an appropriate summary, accounting for paired tasks or repeated runs if applicable. Use a spreadsheet or a short reproducible script, then check the calculations against the raw records.

4. The run log and an independently reproducible calculation would show whether the claims match the evidence. The product owner’s decision is a separate judgment, informed by the measured tradeoff and uncertainty.

```text
Using the run-level experiment records, write a Telegram message to the product owner, a smart non-programmer who reads on a phone. Report honestly whether rewriting each task before execution improved accepted-answer share and what it cost in paid tokens. Include the comparison and uncertainty only to the extent the records support them. State clearly that 48 runs on a task set too easy to show any gain provide a weak measurement; do not imply proof of no effect. If the records do not support a precise estimate, say so plainly rather than inventing one. End with a concrete next-step choice that lets the owner decide whether to stop, keep the trick, or test it on harder tasks. Make the message self-contained, at most 120 words, and return only the message.
```
